shared_context: Consumer query: Do fissures and hemorrhoids heal on their own?

snippets.output: Most hemorrhoids are self-limiting and can heal on their own over time.
snippets.pattern_notes: Two parallel properties of hemorrhoids (self-limiting, heal over time).

snippets.output: Not all hemorrhoids and not all fissures have the potential to heal spontaneously.
snippets.pattern_notes: Parallel claims about hemorrhoids and fissures sharing the property of not always healing spontaneously.

snippets.output: Studies have shown that most small, internal hemorrhoids (grade 1 or 2) can resolve on their own without treatment within 1-2 months.
snippets.notes: Atom 5 was labeled false in input likely because the time-window qualifier was missing; the merged statement with 1-2 months is reasonable.
snippets.pattern_notes: Enumeration of properties of small internal hemorrhoids: can resolve without treatment, within 1-2 months, study-backed.

snippets.output: Larger internal hemorrhoids (grade 3 or 4) and those with significant prolapse may not heal without treatment and may require medical or surgical intervention.
snippets.pattern_notes: Parallel properties of larger/prolapsed hemorrhoids: may not heal, may require intervention.

snippets.output: Most acute anal fissures can heal on their own within 6-8 weeks, though the healing process can be prolonged in some cases.
snippets.pattern_notes: Properties of acute anal fissures: typical healing window plus possible prolongation.

snippets.output: A study found that 80% of patients with acute fissures achieved healing within 6 weeks, while the remaining 20% required additional treatment.
snippets.notes: Atoms 16 and 17 are the un-cited versions of 15 and 18; merged together as one study finding.
snippets.pattern_notes: Enumeration of study findings on acute fissures (80% healed, 20% needed additional treatment).

snippets.output: Chronic fissures may not heal without treatment and may require medical or surgical intervention; one study found that about 10% of patients with chronic fissures did not heal after conservative treatment and required surgical intervention.
snippets.notes: Real-world failure rates for conservative therapy of chronic anal fissures are typically higher (often 30-50%); the 10% figure may be an underestimate but is presented as a single study finding.
snippets.pattern_notes: Enumerated properties of chronic fissures (may not heal, may require intervention) supported by study statistics.
